AI for small business: where do you actually start?

A practical starting point for Melbourne business owners who know AI could help but aren’t sure what to do first.

By Ben Young · Business owner & AI consultant
Updated 16 November 2026

On this page
  • Look for friction in an ordinary working day
  • Separate AI tasks from simple automation
  • Choose one small pilot
  • Bring the people who do the work into the decision
  • A local starting point

When you’re running a small business, finding time to investigate AI is a job in itself. The useful starting point is the work your team repeats every week. Identify a task that takes too long, understand why, and decide what would make it better.

Look for friction in an ordinary working day

Ask the person answering enquiries, scheduling jobs or preparing invoices to walk you through yesterday. Where did they copy information? What did they chase? What sat waiting because only one person knew what to do?

Write down three tasks, how often each happens and roughly how long it takes. For a trade business, that might be turning site notes into reports, copying enquiry details into job software, or searching old emails for customer instructions.

Separate AI tasks from simple automation

Moving an approved customer address between two systems may only need an integration. Turning a messy set of job notes into a readable draft is a possible AI task. The distinction matters: a reliable, simple connection can be more useful than adding AI to a process that doesn’t need it.

Choose one small pilot

  1. Define the task. Be specific about where it starts and finishes.
  2. Record a baseline. Measure time spent, errors or rework before changing anything.
  3. Choose a reviewer. Someone needs to check the output and flag mistakes.
  4. Try representative examples. Include incomplete notes and unusual jobs, not just easy cases.
  5. Compare the result. Count the review time as well as the time saved.

Bring the people who do the work into the decision

A useful tool needs to fit the working day. If a technician has to fill in three extra screens to save someone else a few minutes, the whole process may be worse. Get feedback early and make it easy to report a problem.

For our first conversation: bring one example of repetitive work, a list of the systems involved and a rough idea of how often it happens. You don’t need a technical brief.

A local starting point
